title: How do you handle a database transaction that succeeds but event publishing fails?
description: Solve the atomicity gap between database commits and message-bus publishes using the transactional outbox pattern.

data.text: This is the classic atomicity problem across two different systems. You have a SQL transaction that commits successfully — the order is saved in your database. But when you try to publish an OrderCreated event to a message broker, it fails: the broker is down, the network blips, or the message is malformed. The database change is permanent, but downstream services never learned about it. Your system is now inconsistent.
The interviewer wants to know if you recognize the atomicity gap and can describe the standard pattern that closes it. That pattern is the Transactional Outbox.

Instead of publishing the event directly after the database commit, you write the event to an Outbox table inside the same database transaction. If the transaction commits, the event is guaranteed to be stored. If the transaction rolls back, neither the business data nor the event exist. A separate relay process reads pending outbox records and publishes them to the message broker.

data.title: SQL Server: Outbox table schema
data.code:
CREATE TABLE Outbox (
    Id            UNIQUEIDENTIFIER DEFAULT NEWID() PRIMARY KEY,
    AggregateId   UNIQUEIDENTIFIER NOT NULL,
    EventType     NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    Payload       NVARCHAR(MAX) NOT NULL,
    Status        NVARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    CreatedAt     DATETIME2 NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME(),
    PublishedAt   DATETIME2 NULL
);

CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Outbox_Status_Created
ON Outbox (Status, CreatedAt);

data.text: Both the business data insert and the outbox insert must happen in the same transaction. In EF Core, you add the outbox record to the DbContext alongside your domain entity and call SaveChangesAsync once.

data.title: C#: Saving an order and its outbox event together

data.text: A background worker or hosted service polls for pending outbox records, publishes each one, and marks it as published. To avoid duplicates, use the broker's native deduplication or include the outbox Id as the message key. If publishing fails, the record stays pending and will be retried on the next poll.

cards.title: Transactional Outbox
cards.description: Write events to a database table in the same transaction as business data. Relay publishes them asynchronously.
pros: Strong consistency guarantee within one database

cards.title: Two-Phase Commit
cards.description: A coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then commits or rolls back globally.

cards.title: Eventual Consistency with Compensation
cards.description: Accept temporary inconsistency and reconcile later with compensating transactions.
cons: Not suitable for financial use cases without additional safeguards

data.title: Idempotency still matters
data.text: Even with the outbox pattern, design consumers to handle duplicates. Network retries and relay restarts can redeliver messages. Idempotent consumers are a second layer of defense.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The atomicity gap between database commits and message publishes is solved by the transactional outbox.
Write events to an Outbox table inside the same transaction as business data.
A background relay publishes pending records and handles retries and dead-lettering.
Always keep consumers idempotent as a safety net against redelivered messages.
data.takeaway: Store the intent to publish before you act on the intent.
